titulo.texto: Plumbate Vessel of a Coyote Warrior with a Mother-of-Pearl Beard

frase_gancho.texto: Clay that gleams like metal and traveled from the south.

puente_narrativo.texto: This vessel may once have held precious liquids. The next figure received other gifts: on its belly sits a plate that awaited copal, blood, and hearts. Continue to a reclining man who watches you from the side.

guion_corto.texto: Before you is one of the most singular jewels of Tula: a small vessel thirteen centimeters tall, made of lead-colored ceramic, or “plumbate,” whose gray and orange sheen looks like metal even though it is fired clay. But the most astonishing thing is its face: from the open jaws of a coyote emerges the face of a bearded figure, perhaps linked to Quetzalcóatl or to a warrior chief, covered with a very fine mosaic of mother-of-pearl, abalone, bone, and obsidian. The vessel was made in the Soconusco, on the border between Chiapas and Guatemala, more than a thousand kilometers away, and in Tula a master lapidary clothed it in shell to place it as an offering in the circular temple of El Corral.

guion_largo.texto:
Let us begin with a misunderstanding. The first archaeologists who saw this ceramic, with its metallic gray sheen, thought it was made with lead, and they gave it the name plumbate, from the Latin word for lead, or “lead-colored” in Spanish. They were wrong. Modern analyses showed that it contains no lead: the sheen comes from a very fine clay, rich in iron and aluminum, which was applied as a slip before firing. Today it is still called that, out of tradition.

The process was difficult. The clay was polished with a smooth stone until it was almost like a mirror, and then the piece was fired at very high temperatures, in an atmosphere with little oxygen. The result is a hard, waterproof, almost glassy surface with a metallic look. All of this without a potter’s wheel, without brick kilns, and without metals. It is a technical feat that still amazes ceramists today.

Plumbate ceramics were made in a very specific region: the Soconusco, along the Pacific coast, between southern Chiapas and Guatemala. It was cacao country, the seed from which the drink of the nobles was made and which was used as currency. Centuries later, the Soconusco would become a province that paid tribute to the Mexica, in cacao and in precious feathers. This vessel is a first link in that history.

The distance is what impresses most. From the Soconusco to Tula it is more than a thousand kilometers. Plumbate vessels have been found from Costa Rica to central Mexico, which tells us of merchants who carried these fragile objects on their backs for weeks. They were not cheap goods: they were luxury for the elites. Whoever owned a plumbate vessel showed that their connections reached to the other side of the known world.

The form of this piece is that of an effigy: a vessel that represents a figure. The museum links it with Quetzalcóatl. Plumbate ceramics often bear figures of animals and human beings, sometimes with fantastic features. We know they were used for drinking or for serving liquids, and that the smallest ones may have held highly prized beverages.

And who is Quetzalcóatl in Tula? He is not only a Feathered Serpent as in Teotihuacán: he is also a priest-king, Ce Ácatl Topiltzin Quetzalcóatl, “One Reed, our prince, feathered serpent.” His name combines a birth date and a title. Many historians doubt that he was a real person; others believe there was a ruler who took the name of the god. In any case, the image of the god and that of the king became blurred together.

Look at the sheen of the surface. In Mesoamerica, metalworking arrived late and developed mainly in the West. For that reason, a metallic gleam like this one was extremely rare on the Highlands. The vessel was a way of having the look of a precious metal without possessing it.

Pause for a moment on the central idea: a container the size of a hand that tells us cities did not live alone. Tula, the great military capital, needed the cacao, the feathers, and the shells from the south and from the seas. The wars depicted on the friezes were fed by trade.

texto: Observe the metallic sheen of the plumbate ceramic
Notice the beard and mustache made of shining plaques of mother-of-pearl and abalone shell
Look for the white bone fangs of the coyote that frame the human face

texto.Culture: Toltec (ceramic imported from the Soconusco, Chiapas-Guatemala)
texto.Material: Plumbate ceramic with a mosaic of mother-of-pearl, abalone shell, bone, and obsidian
texto.Origin: Offering from the circular temple of El Corral, Tula, Hidalgo (found by Jorge R. Acosta)
texto.Dimensions: 13 cm high x 9.6 cm wide x 7 cm in diameter

texto.respuesta: Reality: It contains no lead: its sheen comes from a clay very rich in iron, applied as a slip and fired at high temperature.
